title: Reason and Fiat in Case Law
description: Lon L. Fuller — Reason and Fiat in Case Law (59 Harv. L. Rev. 376, 1946)
show_notes:
Lon L. Fuller — Reason and Fiat in Case Law (59 Harv. L. Rev. 376, 1946)

Lon Fuller takes Benjamin Cardozo's jurisprudence as the occasion for examining what he calls the antinomy of reason and fiat — the fact that law is at once an order discovered in the conditions of social life and an order imposed by authority, and that neither branch can be dissolved into the other. He argues that both the extreme natural-law school and the extreme positivists err in trying to eliminate one branch, working the problem through Holmes's identification of a right with a remedy, Ferrero's account of power that must be legitimated, and the American labor boards, whose members conceived of themselves not as decision-makers but as "decision finders." Fuller closes by arguing that the whole view of law is not merely more accurate but more conducive to compromise and tolerance, since a man who believes himself answerable to an external order can admit a mistake without admitting that he is changing himself.
